title: Decode String
description: Brute force to optimized: recursive bracket matching versus an iterative stack based decoder.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an encoded string s in the format k[encoded_string], where the encoded_string inside the brackets is repeated exactly k times, decode it back into its fully expanded form. Encodings can be nested inside each other.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: Given an encoded string s in the format k[encoded_string], where the encoded_string inside the brackets is repeated exactly k times, decode it back into its fully expanded form. Encodings can be nested inside each other.

blocks.title: Analogy: Unpacking Nested Instructions on a Recipe Card
blocks.text: Like following a recipe card that says "repeat this whole sub-step 3 times," where that sub-step might itself contain another "repeat 2 times" instruction nested inside it, needing to be fully unpacked from the innermost instruction outward.

blocks.caption: A number just before brackets means repeat everything inside those brackets that many times

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["3[a] expands to \"aaa\"","2[bc] expands to \"bcbc\"","each bracketed group repeats its own contents independently"],["Concatenated together","\"aaabcbc\"","the two independently expanded groups sit side by side in the output"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Inner 2[c] expands first, to \"cc\"","giving \"3[acc]\"","a nested bracket must be fully resolved before the group containing it can be repeated"],["Then 3[acc] expands to \"accaccacc\"","the nested repetition is fully unpacked","the whole inner result \"acc\" is what gets repeated 3 times, not just \"a\" or just \"c\""]]}

blocks.text: Multiple independent encoded groups, plus plain characters, can appear one after another: 2[abc] becomes "abcabc", 3[cd] becomes "cdcdcd", and "ef" stays as is, giving "abcabccdcdcdef".
It helps to ask exactly what information is needed to resume the outer level once a nested bracket has finished expanding.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The brute force recursively searches forward for the exact matching closing bracket every single time an opening bracket is found, including separately for every nested one, rescanning overlapping regions of the string repeatedly.

Observation 2: Max Chunks to Make Sorted II already showed that a stack can replace explicit index tracking by saving just enough state to resume correctly later, rather than computing exact boundaries up front.

Observation 3: Here, the state worth saving at every opening bracket is exactly two things, the pending repeat count and whatever had already been built at the outer level before this nested section began, pushing that pair and starting fresh removes any need to locate a matching bracket index at all.

Observation 4: A closing bracket then simply pops that saved pair and combines it with whatever was freshly built inside, confirmed by tracing s equal to "3[a2[c]]" through the stack, which correctly unwinds from the innermost "2[c]" outward to the final answer, "accaccacc", in a single left to right pass with no rescanning.

Recognizing that a stack only needs to save the pending count and the outer string built so far, not an exact matching bracket index, is what replaces repeated bracket-matching scans with a single linear pass.

Whenever an opening bracket is found, search forward character by character to locate its exact matching closing bracket, recursively decode everything in between, and then repeat that decoded result the indicated number of times. Since this search for the matching bracket happens independently every time a bracket is encountered, including for every nested bracket, the same regions of the string end up being rescanned repeatedly.

items: Scan the string looking for digits, which indicate an upcoming repeat count.
Once an opening bracket is found, scan forward character by character, tracking nested bracket depth, until its exact matching closing bracket is located.
Recursively decode everything between the brackets, then repeat that result the given number of times.
Continue scanning from just after the matching closing bracket.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Tracking bracket depth while scanning forward is what correctly identifies the true matching closing bracket, even when other brackets are nested in between.
The recursive call decodes only the substring strictly between the matched brackets, so nested encodings are resolved from the inside out automatically.
Scanning resumes immediately after the matched closing bracket, so plain characters and further encoded groups following it are still processed correctly.

blocks.text: Every bracket pair is correctly matched (even when nested), and every repeat count is applied to the fully decoded inner content, so the final expansion is correct.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times d) in the worst case, where d is the nesting depth, since matching brackets and recursing can rescan overlapping regions.
Space: O(n times d), for the recursion stack and the intermediate decoded strings at each level.

Limitation: the recursive bracket matching approach works, but an iterative version using an explicit stack avoids the recursive call overhead and keeps the logic entirely in one single left to right pass.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: locating each matching closing bracket requires its own forward scan, and this repeats independently for every nested bracket, rescanning parts of the string more than once.

What saving state on a stack fixes directly: instead of computing where a bracket pair ends up front, saving the pending count and outer string at the moment of the opening bracket lets processing continue straight through, resolving each level exactly when its closing bracket is reached.

What a closing bracket then needs to do: pop the saved count and outer string, repeat the just finished inner string that many times, and reattach it to the outer string, exactly reversing what was saved.

The core idea: one single left to right pass, pushing state at every opening bracket and popping and combining at every closing bracket, with no bracket matching search ever needed.

Use a stack to hold, at each nesting level, the repeat count and the string built so far at that level. Walk through the string exactly once, left to right. On an opening bracket, push the current count and the string built so far onto the stack and start fresh. On a closing bracket, pop the count and previous string, repeat the just finished inner string that many times, and append it onto the popped previous string.
A single left to right pass using a stack of (count, previous string) pairs.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Character","Action","Stack / current string state"],"rows":[["3","start building a count","count so far: 3"],["[","push (3, \"\") onto the stack, reset current string","stack: [(3, \"\")], current: \"\""],["a","append to current string","current: \"a\""],["2","start building a new count","count so far: 2"],["[","push (2, \"a\") onto the stack, reset current string","stack: [(3, \"\"), (2, \"a\")], current: \"\""],["c","append to current string","current: \"c\""],["]","pop (2, \"a\"), repeat \"c\" twice, append to \"a\"","stack: [(3, \"\")], current: \"acc\""],["]","pop (3, \"\"), repeat \"acc\" three times, append to \"\"","stack: [], current: \"accaccacc\""]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: a stack of pending counts and partial strings, combined on every closing bracket

blocks.text: This works because every opening bracket saves exactly the information needed to resume its outer level later, and every closing bracket restores that exact information, so nesting to any depth is handled correctly simply by the stack growing and shrinking, with no separate bookkeeping of bracket positions required.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["An opening bracket is encountered","The current pending count and the string built so far are pushed, then both reset","The next nested level starts fresh, with its outer context safely preserved"],["A closing bracket is encountered","The saved count and outer string are popped and combined with the just finished inner string","The nested level's result is folded back into its outer context, exactly reversing the push"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times the maximum repeat count), since each character's final expanded appearance is produced exactly once as the stack unwinds.
Space: O(n), for the stack and the output.

blocks.text: This is a classic showcase for the stack based "save state, go deeper, restore and combine" pattern used for any nested bracket structure, whether decoding strings, evaluating nested arithmetic expressions, or parsing nested file paths.

items: Forgetting to reset both the running count and the current string buffer immediately after pushing them onto the stack at an opening bracket.
Reading a multi digit repeat count as only its first digit, instead of accumulating every digit before the bracket.

blocks.text: Draw the stack state at each bracket transition on a whiteboard for a nested example, since visualizing exactly what gets pushed and combined at each step is what makes this pattern click.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid searching for matching brackets", think: a stack that saves the pending count and outer string at every opening bracket instead.
If the interviewer says "what about deeply nested input", think: the stack grows and shrinks naturally with nesting depth, with no special handling needed.
If the interviewer says "how would you evaluate nested arithmetic expressions", think: the same save-state-go-deeper-restore-and-combine stack pattern applies directly.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force (recursive bracket matching): O(n times nesting depth) time, O(n times nesting depth) space. Optimized (iterative stack): O(n times maximum repeat count) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: a stack holding, at each nesting level, the pending repeat count and the string built before that level began.

Core Idea: saving exactly the count and outer string at every opening bracket, then popping and combining at every closing bracket, resolves any nesting depth in a single left to right pass with no explicit bracket matching.
Time: O(n times nesting depth) for the brute force, O(n times maximum repeat count) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n times nesting depth) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: a stack can replace explicit index-based bracket matching entirely, by saving only the minimal state needed to resume the outer level later.
Interview Difficulty: the stack pattern itself is standard once seen; correctly resetting the count and current string buffer at every push is the detail most likely to be forgotten.
One line memory trick: push count and outer string on an open bracket, pop and combine on a close bracket.
